The accident airplane had also been modified from its certificated configuration with a significantly more powerful and heavier engine (Lycoming O-290-D2, 135 hp) than originally specified (Continental O-200-A, 100 hp), likely altering the structural loading and flight characteristics beyond whatever undocumented margins existed in the original design. Witness observations of the left wing separating first, followed by the right wing, during a level-off from a banking turn are consistent with an aerodynamic/structural overload failure of a wing structure of unknown and unverified strength. Missing logbooks precluded determination of the airframe's inspection and maintenance history, and pilot toxicology showed a sedating muscle relaxant (cyclobenzaprine) and other substances, though their role in the loss of control (versus resulting from it) could not be determined. The probable cause is the in-flight failure of the wing structure due to inadequate/unverified structural design of the experimental amateur-built airplane, compounded by an engine modification that increased weight and power beyond the original design basis.
